title: What was happening in the world the last time F1 raced in Malaysia?
excerpt:
Formula 1 returns to Sepang this week for the first time in nine years, with the Malaysian circuit hosting the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The last time F1 raced at Sepang was in 2017, when Lewis Hamilton and Sebastian Vettel were fighting for the Drivers’ Championship, Max Verstappen had just turned 20 and several of the drivers on today’s grid had yet to make their debuts.

Away from the track, Dua Lipa was climbing the charts with New Rules, and Harry Styles had released his first solo album, while IT and Kingsman: The Golden Circle were among the biggest films in cinemas.

As F1 prepares to return to Malaysia, here is a look back at what was happening the last time Formula 1 visited Sepang.

A very different Formula 1 grid

Hamilton arrived in Malaysia leading the Drivers’ Championship, holding a 28-point advantage over Vettel with six races remaining.

The title fight had taken a significant turn at the previous round in Singapore, where Vettel, Kimi Raikkonen and Verstappen were involved in a first-lap collision while Hamilton went on to take victory.

The grid arriving at Sepang also looked very different to the one returning this week. Verstappen was partnered by Daniel Ricciardo at Red Bull, Vettel and Raikkonen formed Ferrari’s line-up, and Fernando Alonso was racing alongside Stoffel Vandoorne at McLaren.

5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Bahrain GP

Carlos Sainz was driving for Toro Rosso [now Racing Bulls], and Pierre Gasly was making his Formula 1 debut with the team that weekend. Charles Leclerc also appeared in FP1 for Sauber, several months before making his Grand Prix debut in 2018.

For Verstappen, there was another reason to remember the weekend. He turned 20 on the Saturday before passing Hamilton to win the race the following day, taking the second victory of his career.

Hamilton finished second ahead of Ricciardo, while Vettel recovered from the back of the grid to take fourth. Hamilton left Malaysia with his advantage in the standings increased to 34 points and would go on to secure his fourth Drivers’ Championship later that year.

Who was topping the charts?

The music charts offer another snapshot of just how long ago 2017 now feels. On the weekend of the Malaysian Grand Prix, Sam Smith’s Too Good at Goodbyes was number one in the UK, with Post Malone and 21 Savage’s rockstar just behind. Dua Lipa’s New Rules sat at number three, while Camila Cabello and Young Thug’s Havana was fourth.

Elsewhere, Taylor Swift was at the beginning of her Reputation era after releasing Look What You Made Me Do in August, while Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee’s Despacito had spent much of the year dominating charts around the world.

Harry Styles had also released his first solo album earlier that year, while Lorde’s Melodrama became one of the defining albums of 2017. The race weekend had its own soundtrack too. Sepang hosted the F1NALE Concert across Saturday and Sunday, with Malaysian artists including M. Nasir, Jaclyn Victor and Akim & The Majistret performing.

What was everyone watching?

Anyone heading to the cinema over the same weekend could have watched Kingsman: The Golden Circle, which was number one at the UK box office between September 29 and October 1. The horror film IT, starring Bill Skarsgård as Pennywise, was in second place.

Several of the films that would become synonymous with 2017 had already arrived by then. Disney’s live-action Beauty and the Beast was released in March, followed later in the year by Wonder Woman, Spider-Man: Homecoming, Baby Driver and Christopher Nolan’s Dunkirk. Jordan Peele’s Get Out had also reached cinemas earlier in the year, while The Greatest Showman was still a few months away.

On television, Stranger Things still had just one season available, with its second about to arrive later in October. Game of Thrones had only recently finished its seventh and penultimate season, while Riverdale and The Handmaid’s Tale had both made their debuts earlier in 2017.

Who was winning trophies elsewhere?

In football, Real Madrid won both the UEFA Champions League and La Liga, with Cristiano Ronaldo claiming another Ballon d'Or – his fifth and final one – alongside the FIFA Best Men's Player award‌. The Portuguese legend has been a frequent spectator at F1 events over the years.

Hosts the Netherlands won the 2017 Women’s Euros, with Vivianne Miedema – now of Manchester City – scoring twice in the final for a 4-2 win over Denmark.

In tennis, Roger Federer was enjoying a remarkable renaissance, winning the Australian Open and Wimbledon, the latter for a record eighth time. The Swiss superstar has since returned to SW19 as a spectator – and this year he sat beside Kimi Antonelli, giving him some advice on how to handle the pressure of elite sport.

Rafael Nadal underlined his credentials as the king of clay when he extended his record to ten French Open triumphs, helping him to the year-end No. 1 spot. Serena Williams was also breaking records on court, winning in Melbourne for her 23rd Grand Slam title, the most in the women’s game during the Open Era.

Elsewhere, in athletics, Usain Bolt’s competitive career came to an emotional end as he finished third in the 100m and suffered an injury in the 4x100m relay at the World Championships in London. Incidentally, the Jamaican is a big F1 fan, and a huge supporter of Hamilton.

And in golf, Sergio Garcia finally won his first major championship at The Masters. It was his 74th attempt, and came in a sudden-death play-off against Justin Rose.

What was changing in the world of tech?

It was also a landmark year for electric cars, mobile phones, and even drones. Some of those milestone product launches proved to be game-changers: 2017 marked the beginning of the end for home-screen buttons as Apple launched the iPhone X, while orders for the newly-launched Tesla Model 3 far outstripped supply. Other products such as Jibo – the pet robot who featured on the cover of Time Magazine – failed to stick around.

It was the year of the Nintendo Switch, the dawn of 3D-printed Adidas trainers and saw the arrival of relatively affordable drones, sparking the craze for bird’s eye-view ‘dronies’ captured at exotic locations.

And six-second video app Vine was fading from memory having been officially shut down on 17 January 2017.

Why a return to Sepang is a 'golden ticket' for F1 drivers

What were we wearing?

Fashion and cosmetics also experienced sea-change moments in 2017. Rihanna played a central consulting role in her Fenty Beauty make-up range, with its 40 foundation shades celebrated for the diverse palette of skin tones, saying, “It was important that every woman felt included.”

Crocs started to become ‘trendy’ – a word used lightly – after they had previously only been used in the garden or for taking out the bins. They were now appearing in a variety of colours, designs and offered fun personalisation through their expanding range of Jibbitz.

Platform clogs were even a thing, and other varieties appeared at London Fashion Week.

Tights being exposed through jeans was also a look, and so were boots that are also like socks.

Corsets also started to appear more through social media stars, as well as in music videos like Little Mix's Touch where they opted to layer it over a jumper.

Nine years later, (some of) the drivers, sporting stars, technology, fashion and pop culture may have changed, but one thing will be familiar this week as Formula 1 cars return to Sepang once again.

title: Why there’s still hope for Russell in the 2026 title race
excerpt:
George Russell cut Kimi Antonelli’s championship lead from 81 points to 66 at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, bringing him back into the title race conversation after he had ruled himself out of it. Can the Briton build on that swing at the Bahrain Grand Prix and beyond, and become a genuine contender once more? F1.com runs through the factors working in his favour…

Plenty of points still to play for

As things stand, there are eight rounds remaining in the 2026 F1 season – including a Sprint weekend at the Singapore Grand Prix.

It means that the maximum overall points score still available is 208, which would be achieved by a driver winning every Grand Prix as well as the Sprint.

Heading to the Sepang International Circuit, Antonelli sits at the top of the Drivers’ Championship standings on 302 points, with Russell – as mentioned – 66 adrift on a total of 236.

On paper, this leaves plenty of time and opportunity for Russell to turn the tables with a late-season charge, though the Briton would need to outscore his Italian counterpart by an average of 8.25 points per round (before factoring in victory and other results countback).

An element hanging over Russell is that he looks set to take a grid penalty for new power unit components at one of the final rounds – something Antonelli got out of the way ahead of his stunning P19-P1 charge at Monza.

Russell’s got history at upcoming tracks

With victory in Baku, Russell now has eight Grand Prix wins to his name. Three of those were achieved at tracks still to come on the 2026 schedule, and are regarded as some of his best drives in the sport so far.

In 2022, Russell earned his maiden triumph at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, impressively sustaining late-race pressure from seven-time World Champion team mate Lewis Hamilton, and in 2024, he dominated from start to finish around the streets of Las Vegas.

Then, in 2025, Russell earned redemption at the Singapore Grand Prix (after a painful last-lap crash in 2023) with a particularly satisfying pole position-to-victory performance, after which Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff praised his “formidable” level.

We are, of course, under a different set of regulations, with driver and car form fluctuating across each season, but Russell at least has some good memories to lean into as he approaches this decisive phase of the campaign.

Why Russell “feels like myself again”

On the topic of regulations, Russell has spoken openly about his struggles to get the most out of F1’s new generation of cars, with overhauled aerodynamics, revised power units and various driver-controlled modes all being introduced.

It started so well with pole and victory at the season opener in Australia, but after that, Russell went through periods of confusion and frustration, as well as suffering his fair share of misfortune, all while team mate Antonelli stormed to poles and wins.

Since the summer break, Russell appears to have made some progress, as he pointed to in Azerbaijan, where he took pole position by more than eight tenths of a second, and kept a charging Max Verstappen at bay for his first win since June.

“I’m very proud of the resilience that I and my close group of engineers have shown during the tough periods this year, because there’s been a lot of hard work to overcome some of the challenges, to adapt my driving style to suit this new car better,” said Russell.

“F1 is so tough, you don’t get opportunities to practice this, and finally it’s coming to me a bit more intuitively than it once did, and I’m gaining confidence. Especially on circuits like this, it just allows you to eke out that little bit more on the brakes, and get that little bit closer to the walls, and it’s been a flawless weekend.”

He continued: “I think I never lost that faith in myself. Even through the tough moments, I knew there was a reason why I was off the pace. It wasn’t like I just suddenly forgot how to drive, and I knew I would be able to find it again. I just had to be patient.”

Driving with the pressure off

Antonelli is clearly favourite to seal the 2026 drivers’ title over the remaining sequence of races given his 66-point buffer, which would allow him to take the next two race weekends off and still hold at least an eight-point advantage.

A crash during Q1 in Baku marked one of the youngster’s few mistakes of the season, however, with Russell commenting afterwards that “there’s much less pressure on me than there is him” as the final flyaway events tick by.

Asked how he is approaching the run-in, as the hunter rather than the hunted, Russell replied: “Win every race. I mean, that’s the game plan. My team mate’s had an incredible season, he’s been pretty flawless throughout, but now we’re getting to crunch time.”

He added: “I didn’t really consider myself in this fight for a number of races, purely because my performance wasn’t strong enough. If the season were to have started today, or since the summer break, I feel very much I would have been able to fight.

“Now I’ve got this big deficit. It can change quickly, so I’m not chasing that. I’m chasing to win every race, and what will be, will be.”

title: Facts, stats and trivia ahead of the 2026 Bahrain GP
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season continues this weekend as Sepang hosts Round 16 on the calendar, the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Free Practice 1 and 2 will take place on Friday, October 2, followed by Free Practice 3 and Qualifying on Saturday, October 3, and the Grand Prix itself on Sunday, October 4.

Vital statistics

First Grand Prix – 1999 (as the Malaysian Grand Prix)

Track Length – 5.543km

Lap record – 1m 34.080s, Sebastian Vettel, Ferrari, 2017

Most pole positions – Lewis Hamilton and Michael Schumacher (5)

Most wins – Sebastian Vettel (4)

Trivia – Sepang was the first F1 track to be designed by renowned circuit architect Hermann Tilke

Overtakes completed in 2017 – 73

Safety Car probability – 20%*

Virtual Safety Car probability – 20%*

Pit stop time loss – 23.7 seconds

*From the last five Grands Prix at Sepang

The driver’s verdict

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver: Sepang is a brilliantly flowing lap, with a fast middle sector splintering big braking zones with plenty of switchback opportunity.

Turn 1 is extremely wide and it’s important to attack the brakes before getting back to hug a late apex to get nicely out of the tighter Turn 2 and up the following curved straight.

The middle sector is all about high-speed balance and flow. A committed entry is needed on the entry for the incredibly high-speed run through 5 before picking your change of direction perfectly into 6 as the track drops away slightly. This is the highest speed cornering section on the circuit. Turn 7 is a bit slower and easy to run wide on the exit before the final part of that sequence which should be an acceleration zone if executed right.

Braking for both Turns 11 and 14 are tricky and all about feel as you are coaxing the car through right hand bends on approach, especially for 14 where it’s easy to lock the right front. Again, the exit of this corner is critical, leading into the final big stamp on the brakes and an overtaking chance at the final turn.

All you need to know about the Sepang International Circuit

Last five Bahrain GP polesitters

2025 – Oscar Piastri (McLaren)

2024 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2023 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2022 – Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

2021 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Last five Bahrain GP winners

2025 – Oscar Piastri (McLaren)

2024 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2023 – Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2022 – Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)

2021 – Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

Tyre and strategy insight

“Sepang features a relatively abrasive surface, with a level of roughness comparable to Bahrain, while retaining its own distinctive characteristics,” reads Pirelli’s weekend preview. “Grip levels are likely to be low on Friday but should improve progressively over the course of the weekend as the track evolves. One of the main challenges facing teams will be thermal management across both axles.

“The circuit has undergone several changes in recent years. In 2023, the section between Turns 6 and 12 was resurfaced, with further work carried out in the area around Turn 9. However, the overall characteristics of the surface, as assessed by Pirelli engineers just a few weeks ago, remain very similar to those recorded in 2017.

“More recently, from the beginning of September, additional surface levelling work was carried out to remove irregularities in the asphalt, alongside cleaning operations aimed at improving track conditions ahead of the World Championship event.

“Teams will also have to contend with a lack of available data. Despite being a historic venue, no team possesses truly relevant references relating to the current generation of Formula 1 cars.

"As a result, Friday practice sessions will be more important than usual, both for drivers, who will need to familiarise themselves with a circuit that many have only experienced in the simulator, and for teams, which must identify the correct car balance and assess tyre behaviour.

“While there is no shortage of technical unknowns, the weather could add a further layer of complexity. Afternoon thunderstorms are a regular feature of the region in early October and could affect any session during the weekend. Intense heat, high humidity and sudden downpours have always been among the defining characteristics of the Malaysian Grand Prix during its years as a permanent fixture on the Formula 1 calendar.”

Current Form

Kimi Antonelli remains at the top of the drivers' standings despite a sub-optimal weekend in Baku, where a crash in Qualifying meant the Mercedes did well to salvage fifth in the race.

In contrast, team mate George Russell enjoyed possibly his best weekend of the season, taking a dominant pole before holding off Max Verstappen in the closing stages for his third victory of the year, bringing Antonelli's margin down to 66 points.

Verstappen was just one tenth off his first win of the season, but Red Bull look to be finding form as Isack Hadjar claimed a podium on his return from a wrist injury.

Azerbaijan proved to be a disaster for McLaren as neither driver scored, with reigning World Champion Lando Norris eliminated in a crash, but the Briton has previously proven to be the closest challenger to Mercedes prior to the last round.

Ferrari, meanwhile, left Baku with a double points finish and will be looking to find greater performance to once again challenge for wins.

In the midfield fight, Racing Bulls pulled further ahead of Alpine in the teams' standings as they battle for P5, with Franco Colapinto set to serve a five-place grid penalty in Sepang for the Baku incident that eliminated himself and team mate Pierre Gasly.

Haas will be looking to score more points after the team's first double points finish, while Williams' major upgrade gave Carlos Sainz the chance to finish inside the top 10 for the first time since May.

Iconic Moments in Sepang

There have been no shortage of memorable moments from the Sepang International Circuit over the years, often involving sudden downpours of rain that have caused chaos and produced thrilling races.

But a lack of rain doesn't mean there is no drama, with Red Bull team mates Sebastian Vettel and Mark Webber proving the point in 2013 as the pair went wheel-to-wheel for the win, the former victorious after disobeying team orders.

title: All you need to know about the Sepang International Circuit
excerpt:
After an eventful race in Azerbaijan saw George Russell narrowly beat Max Verstappen, Formula 1 moves straight onto the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. But how much do you know about the Sepang International Circuit? F1.com has your all-in-one guide…

Key Sepang International Circuit statistics

Circuit length: 5.543km

Number of turns: 15

Number of laps: 56

Race distance: 310.398km

Lap record: 1m 34.080s – Sebastian Vettel (2017)

When was Malaysia’s first Grand Prix?

After it was decided that the Bahrain Grand Prix would not take place in its original calendar slot in April, Malaysia stepped up to host the event, shifting it to the first weekend of October.

It will mark the first Grand Prix at the Sepang International Circuit since 2017, but the country’s links with F1 go back to the 1990s, when then-Prime Minister Dr Mahathir Mohamad set about building a first-rate motorsport venue.

Once renowned designer Hermann Tilke had planned the layout, construction began in 1997, with the inaugural race taking place in 1999. It was won by Ferrari’s Eddie Irvine and established Sepang as a fast and challenging track, setting a precedent for other purpose-built circuits.

What’s the circuit like to drive?

Only 10 drivers on the current grid have competed in Malaysia before – that was nearly a decade ago, so while they’ll have an advantage over their younger competitors, it’s likely that there’ll be a steep learning curve for everyone.

Jolyon Palmer, former Renault F1 driver, explained: "Sepang is a brilliantly flowing lap, with a fast middle sector splintering big braking zones with plenty of switchback opportunity.

"Turn 1 is extremely wide and it’s important to attack the brakes before getting back to hug a late apex to get nicely out of the tighter Turn 2 and up the following curved straight.

5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Bahrain GP

"The middle sector is all about high-speed balance and flow. A committed entry is needed on the entry for the incredibly high-speed run through 5 before picking your change of direction perfectly into 6 as the track drops away slightly. This is the highest speed cornering section on the circuit. Turn 7 is a bit slower and easy to run wide on the exit before the final part of that sequence which should be an acceleration zone if executed right.

"Braking for both Turns 11 and 14 are tricky and all about feel as you are coaxing the car through right hand bends on approach, especially for 14 where it’s easy to lock the right front. Again, the exit of this corner is critical, leading into the final big stamp on the brakes and an overtaking chance at the final turn."

If the layout doesn’t sound demanding enough, Sepang is also known for its unpredictable weather – high humidity, extreme heat and sudden downpours have all impacted races in the past.

Where are the Straight Mode zones and overtake detection?

As a reminder, and as explained in our pre-season summary of regulation changes, Straight Mode is a different aerodynamic configuration that allows cars to reduce their drag, making them more efficient when accelerating up towards top speed.

The rear wing continues to open up a gap – just like it did when drivers used DRS (the Drag Reduction System) in the past – but now the front wing also moves. The uppermost front wing elements drop down at the same time the rear wing’s top element does.

This is a mode that is used on every single lap in dry conditions, in every area that is designated for it. Essentially, the car will adapt between two different configurations depending on where it is on the track, providing maximum downforce in corners but then less drag on straights.

In Malaysia, there are four designated Straight Mode zones, beginning with a run along the start/finish straight, then between Turns 3 and 4, between Turns 8 and 9, and finally between Turns 14 and 15.

Meanwhile, Overtake Mode replaces DRS and is a new power mode that allows a driver to recharge more electrical energy, and generate an additional electrical power profile, so they can sustain a higher speed for a longer period.

There is one detection point per lap for this mode – expected to be out of the final corner on many occasions, leading onto a long straight – and it will be available to drivers on the following lap as long as they stay within a second of the car in front at that detection point.

The Overtake Detection marker at the Sepang International Circuit comes as drivers exit Turn 15, while the Overtake Activation line follows at the beginning of the start/finish straight.

Five fun facts about the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia

Lewis Hamilton and Michael Schumacher hold the record for the most pole positions at the Sepang International Circuit, with five apiece

It was the first F1 track designed from scratch by Tilke – he had previously only renovated what is now the Red Bull Ring in Austria

Ferrari’s most recent victory in wet weather came in Malaysia in 2012, when Fernando Alonso won from P8 on the grid

This weekend will mark the 22nd edition of the Bahrain Grand Prix, and the first not to be held at the Bahrain International Circuit in Sakhir

Other countries have stepped in to host races before – the San Marino Grand Prix was held in Italy between 1981 and 2006, the 1997 and 1998 Luxembourg Grands Prix took place in Germany, and the 1982 Swiss Grand Prix was contested in France

title: Hadjar explains what makes Verstappen such a tough driver
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar's sophomore season in Formula 1 has been something of a rollercoaster having been brought into Red Bull alongside Max Verstappen, occupying a spot which many have failed to keep over the years.

The Frenchman's impressive debut campaign in 2025, which included a podium at Zandvoort, certainly caught the attention of the Red Bull hierarchy and Hadjar has slowly adapted to the unique challenge – one he relishes – of being Verstappen's team mate in 2026.

A podium at Monaco was eventually confirmed, while another came last weekend in Azerbaijan on his most competitive weekend yet for Red Bull having challenged Verstappen – made even more impressive having missed the three previous races due to a wrist injury.

Speaking on the latest episode of official F1 podcast Beyond the Grid, Hadjar explained what it was like going up against the four-time World Champion in equal machinery.

“I'm probably facing the prime of the prime of the level you can achieve in Formula 1 and he’s just next to me in the garage. To experience this at my age, this early in my career, I'm one very, very lucky guy," said Hadjar.

"He's a very, very kind guy. We get along really well. It's good to work with him. I'm grateful because he gives me so much to work with, to improve, which probably no one else can give. So just for that, I'm thankful and it's great.

“I would say it’s exactly what I expected Max Verstappen to be on the track. I had an idea of how good he was and it translates really well. What I have in my mind that I want to achieve on track, he kind of does it. But there's always a difference between what you're aiming to do and what you actually deliver.

"There's always a little gap sometimes, but he's constant, he doesn't like really have low moments. I would say, it's just like no mistake. He's always at the right time, the right place as well. He creates his own luck a bit.

"But I love the challenge. I love going into every session knowing that he's going to set a benchmark that I need to match and I need to overcome. It's just exciting. It changes from everything I've had my whole career.

“Let's say on a track, you have like 15 corners and maybe there's one corner you master, or two, three, four, five corners, you do really, really well. But he matches you there and then on the others, he keeps that same level.

"And then over the lap, he makes the lap time difference. I wouldn't say I look at the data and I'm like, ‘I can't reproduce this.’ It's how often he does it. That makes the big difference at the end. It's like he has no peak, it’s flat. It's up there, but it's flat. It's what makes him such a tough driver.”

Prior to his best weekend of the season in Baku, Red Bull confirmed they would retain the services of Hadjar for 2027, something backed by Verstappen himself.

Hadjar's aspirations are certainly not lacking, and with a driver of Verstappen's calibre to learn from on the other side of the garage, he hopes more podiums and even wins are not too far away.

"I think so far now I've been doing a good job at being there," said Hadjar on his performances so far.

"But there's still that thing missing... There are a few things that I need to align a bit more. Sometimes it can be a race start that we compromise.

"Sometimes it's that first stint with the heavy car killing the tyres a bit early, being two positions up the grid in qualifying, you're missing half a tenth, and then you have a different Sunday unfortunately. It's all these little things you can align like Max does, and then you're in contention.”

title: Fernando Alonso delivers 'five-minute' declaration over F1 future decision
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso confirmed earlier this week that he will remain with Aston Martin for the 2027 F1 campaign.

Fernando Alonso has stated it took only five minutes of talks with Aston Martin owner Lawrence Stroll before deciding to commit to F1 for another season.

The two-time champion's future was under question amid the team's lack of competitiveness this season under fresh technical regulations.

Following months of speculation, Alonso put the matter to bed earlier this week as he declared he would remain on the grid next year.

It will mark a record-extending 24th campaign on the grid, which is set to make him the first 46-year-old F1 driver in 62 years.

When asked when he reached the decision that he would continue, Alonso told media including RacingNews365: "I don't know, I don't think I have a date.

"I took the decision but it was quite recent. Sitting with Lawrence, it was very straightforward.

"We didn't have much to discuss. We both wanted to continue at that point, and it was a five-minute talk and we announced it."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Fernando Alonso

Spanish

14

Alonso admits to motivation struggles

Aston Martin and its engine supplier Honda have endured a highly challenging campaign, languishing at the back of the field with unconvincing pace and reliability.

Alonso admitted it has been challenging to remain motivated through the tough period.

"Obviously, we are not competitive on the weekends," he said.

"You try to be as professional as you can in the preparations and into the race weekend.

"It would be different if we were fighting for podiums or for wins. We still do our job, our pre-weekend approach and studies about the circuit simulations, all these kind of things, but knowing that the result will not be very competitive.

"That's not helping the motivation. But you know, as you said, at the end of the day, we close the visor, we go racing, and that's enough."

title: Esteban Ocon speaks out on Haas F1 exit: 'I don’t deserve this'
excerpt:
Haas and Esteban Ocon announced in the build-up to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that they would no longer continue in partnership

Esteban Ocon has spoken out for the first time after confirming his exit from the Haas F1 team.

Speculation over the Frenchman's future has been rife for several weeks, with Haas known to be evaluating a handful of contenders for a 2027 F1 seat.

In the build-up to the Bahrain Grand Prix at Sepang, the team confirmed that Ocon would exit at the end of the 2026 campaign.

It will bring his two-year stretch with the team to an end, putting doubt over his future on the grid with limited spaces available for the 2027 season.

As he begins to close out his ninth full season in F1, he admitted it is irritating to be placed in such a position.

"It is frustrating because it's not really the way it should be," Ocon told media including RacingNews365.

"I'm not going to go into detail about what happens in the past. I'm looking ahead, I'm looking at the future.

"That's what's important, but I deserve to be here. I put [in] the hard work.

"We have benefited from finding out all these issues very early, since I joined the team, and it has been very good for everyone.

"I don't think I deserve to have this for the future.

"But there are opportunities all the time in F1, and that's what I'm looking at, looking at the future, not the past."

It means that Ocon will likely have to take on a third driver role next year in order to retain his links in F1.

"My focus is on F1, that is clear," he said. "That's where I belong, that's where I want to be. I'm not going to look elsewhere, that's very clear.

"But you never know what can happen in F1. As you guys know, things move every two seconds, so I'm still working on trying to find a solution for next year.

title: Alpine record major financial profit after previous heavy loss
excerpt:
The Alpine F1 team recorded a profit of £8 million GBP in the financial year ending December 31st, 2025, new documents show.

It comes after the team produced a heavy loss of £14.6 million GBP in the corresponding period to December 31st, 2024.

According to the official financial documents submitted to Companies House, a legal requirement for any company in the UK, 'Alpine Racing Limited' enjoyed a turnover of £287.562 million in the 2025 FY, a sharp rise from £238.508 million GBP in the 12-month period prior.

As with every F1 team, the turnover is calculated by taking the prize money awarded in the constructors' championship as well as commercial sponsors.

The money Alpine received for its sixth-place finish in the 2024 constructors' standings was factored into the 2025 accounts - with the team being boosted by scoring 33 of its 65 points that year in the torrentially wet Sao Paulo GP where Esteban Ocon took second and Pierre Gasly third.

After the prior race in Mexico City, Alpine had found itself ninth in the standings on just 17 points - but climbed to sixth, with Gasly also banking two points for seventh in the Sprint, overhauling Haas and Racing Bulls.

Once cost of sales of £222.378 million was factored in, this left the team with a gross profit of £65.184 million GBP, a climb of £20.713 million GBP year-on-year from 2024.

After other expenses were deducted, it left the team with an operating profit of £16.527 million GBP for the 2025 year.

In 2024, Alpine Racing Limited recorded an operating loss at this stage of £10.192 million GBP.

After UK tax had been applied, it left the team's bottom line figure back in the black by £8.007 million GBP. In the previous year, it had lost £14.625 million GBP, something of an anomaly after strong profits in preceding years.

The submission is one of a number of teams RacingNews365 has examined thus far, including Williams and Aston Martin, as well as F1 itself.

Submissions from Red Bull and McLaren are due imminently, with Mercedes recording its figures ahead of schedule in June.

title: Liam Lawson points out Red Bull truth after surprise super-sub appearances
excerpt:
Liam Lawson believes his three races for Red Bull as a super-sub injury replacement "didn't really change anything" for him in the ecosystem of drivers.

Lawson was called up for the Dutch, Italian, and Spanish Grands Prix as injury cover for Isack Hadjar, with the New Zealander returning to the team he was dropped from after just two tough races in early 2025.

He scored points on two occasions, with a best-of-the-rest seventh at Zandvoort on a weekend Red Bull was the fourth-best team and sixth in Spain before Hadjar returned in Azerbaijan.

Hadjar was then confirmed as Max Verstappen's permanent team-mate for 2027, but when asked whether his strong showing at the senior team had had any impact about a potential re-promotion, Lawson denied this, saying he was never intended to drive the RB22 in 2026.

"I mean, the thing is, I wasn't meant to drive this year for Red Bull," Lawson told media, including RacingNews365, when asked if his performances had changed anything for him within the ecosystem.

"Obviously I've been in the fight with VCARB, and I wasn't looking at it, to be honest.

"It was great to do those races; it was challenging, but it didn't really change anything outside of that for next year.

"It's pretty standard, which is not surprising.

"For me, I didn't come out of last year and question my ability to drive a race car, so it is nice that I've been able to have those races and maybe show the rest of the world [what I am capable of doing].

"But it didn't change anything for me, to be honest."

title: Five things you need to know about the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia
excerpt:
Formula 1 returns to the Sepang International Circuit for round 16 of the season, though the race retains its Bahrain Grand Prix branding after Malaysia stepped in as a substitute host.

First adorning the F1 calendar in 1999, the venue has not hosted F1 since 2017, but its history, layout and climate remain as relevant as ever heading into the weekend. Here are five things worth knowing before the lights go out.

1. Tilke's proving ground

Sepang was the first Formula 1 circuit Hermann Tilke built from scratch, arriving after his redesign of Austria's A1 Ring, the track now known as the Red Bull Ring.

The 1999 project set the template for a career that would go on to shape much of the modern calendar, including the Bahrain International Circuit, Shanghai International Circuit, Istanbul Park, Marina Bay Street Circuit, Yas Marina Circuit, Circuit of the Americas, Baku City Circuit and the Jeddah Corniche Circuit.

The Tilke fingerprint is recognisable across those venues: long straights feeding into sharp, low-speed hairpins designed to encourage overtaking, generous paved run-off to satisfy FIA safety requirements, and flowing multi-apex sequences woven around landmark architecture.

Sepang was where that philosophy was first tested at grand prix level, and much of what followed at Shanghai, Istanbul and Baku traces its roots back to Malaysia.

2. (Almost) half a grid of Sepang veterans

Ten of the 22 drivers on this weekend's entry list have raced at Sepang before, a reminder of how long the circuit has been absent from the calendar despite still carrying recent memories for much of the paddock.

Max Verstappen won the Malaysian Grand Prix the last time F1 visited the Sepang International Circuit, just the second of his now 71 victories.

Of the nine drivers racing this weekend who also competed nine years ago, Hamilton returns to the scene of his 2016 heartbreak; and Fernando Alonso, Valtteri Bottas, Carlos Sainz, Nico Hülkenberg, Esteban Ocon, Sergio Perez, Lance Stroll, and Pierre Gasly — who was making his F1 debut in 2017 — all have prior Malaysian Grand Prix starts on their CVs.

3. The weather wildcard

Sepang's return could hardly come at a more volatile time of year. Late September and early October fall squarely within the monsoon transition period in Malaysia, when air temperatures regularly exceed 30 degrees Celsius, humidity climbs above 70 per cent, and violent afternoon thunderstorms can arrive with little warning.

The circuit's history bears this out: the 2009 race was red-flagged due to torrential rain overwhelming the track's drainage, and the 2012 event suffered a similarly lengthy weather-enforced suspension.

Forecasters covering this week's return have flagged a genuine risk of disruption, and teams will be wary of sudden downpours turning a straightforward strategy into chaos inside a handful of laps.

Given the punishing heat and humidity that typically precede those storms, cooling and tyre management will be under scrutiny long before any rain arrives.

4. A circuit built to reward bravery

Sepang's layout has long been rated among the more driver-friendly on the calendar for wheel-to-wheel racing. Its wide track footprint, stretching between 16 and 25 metres in places, combines with two long back-to-back straights funnelling into a tight hairpin at Turn 15, creating a heavy braking zone that has produced countless overtakes over the years.

The corner profile is unusually varied for a single lap: fast, sweeping sequences through Turns 5 and 6 sit alongside tighter, low-speed corners, downhill braking zones and off-camber apexes.

That mix, combined with abrasive asphalt and the tropical heat, makes Sepang notoriously tough on tyres, with particular stress placed on the shoulders through the circuit's sustained high-speed curves.

The blend of overtaking opportunity and physical tyre demand is part of why so many regard Sepang as one of Tilke's finest pieces of work, even after its 2017 departure from the calendar amid falling ticket sales and rising hosting costs.

This weekend offers a rare chance to see whether that reputation still holds up under a modern grid and a 2026-spec car.

5. A history soaked in drama

The Malaysian Grand Prix ran from 1999 to 2017, and few venues on the calendar have produced chaos quite like Sepang did in its very first year.

Eddie Irvine beat Ferrari team-mate Michael Schumacher to the flag in the inaugural race, a result that kept Irvine's title hopes alive heading into the season finale. But the result did not stand unchallenged for long: post-race scrutineering found both Ferraris' bargeboards in breach of dimensional regulations, and stewards disqualified the entire Ferrari one-two, provisionally handing the win to Mika Häkkinen and, with it, the 1999 drivers' championship, before the season had even reached Suzuka.

Ferrari appealed, and the FIA International Court of Appeal ultimately overturned the disqualifications, ruling that manufacturing tolerances and measurement uncertainty meant the bargeboards were not actually illegal. The one-two was reinstated, Irvine's championship lead was restored, and the title fight went down to the wire in Japan.

Two years later, Sepang produced a race remembered for entirely different reasons. The 2001 Malaysian Grand Prix, only the second round of that season, turned into a lottery on lap three when a localised tropical downpour combined with oil spilt by Olivier Panis to send cars aquaplaning across the circuit, with both leading Ferraris spinning into the gravel at the same moment.

A lengthy safety car period followed while marshals recovered stranded cars, and Ferrari compounded their misfortune with a bungled 72-second double stack caused by misplaced wet tyres, dropping Schumacher and Rubens Barrichello outside the top ten.

But a bold call to fit intermediates rather than full wets as the track began to dry let both drivers slice back through the field, and Schumacher and Barrichello ultimately crossed the line first and second, an extraordinary recovery from a race that had briefly threatened to be a write-off for the team.

The 2009 edition was infamous for being stopped early due to a violent tropical downpour, with the race called before full distance and Jenson Button's Brawn taking a shortened victory.

Then came 2013, when Red Bull's Multi 21 team orders controversy erupted: Sebastian Vettel ignored an instruction to hold station behind Mark Webber and passed him regardless, a move Christian Horner later suggested was partly payback for Webber's conduct during their 2012 title fight in Brazil.

The most consequential Sepang race for the championship picture, though, came in 2016. Lewis Hamilton had qualified on pole and looked set for a crucial win in his fight with Mercedes team-mate Nico Rosberg, only for his power unit to fail with smoke pouring from the rear of his car late in the race.

Mercedes later traced the failure to a crankshaft big-end bearing that gave way without warning after a sudden drop in oil pressure. The result handed Rosberg a 23-point championship lead with five rounds remaining, a 28-point swing from the would-be result, from which Hamilton never recovered. Rosberg went on to claim the title before retiring from the sport days later.

title: Lewis Hamilton identifies two key reasons for F1 to race in Malaysia
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton is thrilled that F1 is returning to the Sepang International Circuit, which is hosting the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Lewis Hamilton has explained why he believes Formula 1 is right to return to the Sepang International Circuit, pointing to the quality of racing the track produces, the "massively physically demanding" nature of the climate — and his own affection for Kuala Lumpur.

The seven-time F1 drivers' champion spoke glowingly about the championship's unexpected return after almost a decade away, ahead of this weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Hamilton has a long history with the country's capital city, having previously raced there with McLaren and then Mercedes, with the German team's title sponsor being Petronas, a company headquartered in Kuala Lumpur.

"I always love going to KL [Kuala Lumpur]," the Ferrari driver told media, including RacingNews365. "Had lots of great experiences there with my previous team, and the track is awesome. It is a circuit that does give good racing."

Hamilton said the calibre of racing on offer should be central to any decision over which circuits remain on the calendar.

"And when it comes to deciding what tracks to go through in the year, that should be a part of the decision-making," he added.

"We want good races for fans, not ones that you don't see any overtaking in, so I very much welcome it."

Physical demands ahead

Hamilton won the Malaysian Grand Prix for Mercedes in 2014, but Sepang has not always been kind to him.

Two years later, he arrived on pole position only to retire with an engine failure while leading, a blow that handed Nico Rosberg a championship advantage he would not relinquish, with Hamilton's Mercedes team-mate going on to clinch that year's title.

Nonetheless, Hamilton is relishing a return. He also flagged the brutal conditions drivers face at Sepang, where daytime temperatures regularly climb well past 30 degrees Celsius with humidity above 80 per cent, sapping the body's ability to cool itself inside the cockpit.

Due to the intensity of the environment, drivers can lose upwards of four kilograms of body weight across the 56-lap race.

"I'm looking forward to it," the 106-time grand prix winner said.

"It's a super hot circuit; it's going to be one that's physically massively demanding, so I look forward to that challenge."

title: Valtteri Bottas claims Cadillac car was 'confused' in strange F1 crash
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas believes his Cadillac F1 car's energy systems became "confused", which led to his crash out of the Azerbaijan GP.

Bottas's race in Baku ended in the Turn 15 wall in the closing laps, with race leaders George Russell and Max Verstappen passing by on the final lap with the incident covered under yellow flags.

The incident appeared weird as Bottas was not travelling at high-speed, with the Finn pointing to an off earlier around the lap as a potential factor in how the car's energy systems had become "confused."

"On the same lap, I had a lock-up going into Turn 1 and went wide," Bottas told media, including RacingNews365.

"Then I think the systems got a bit confused because of the extra distance.

"I had a huge super clip into Turn 15, and then when I hit the brakes, only the front brakes would work.

"It was almost like I wasn't harvesting anymore with the rears, so something got a bit confused there."

F1 drivers do not actually control the energy deployment themselves in 2026.

Rather, a series of on-board algorithms are constantly learning and evolving to best deploy the energy, requiring smooth, consistent inputs from the driver so the system can 'learn' the circuit.

title: Formula E hand F1 bombshell claim: ‘We will be faster’
excerpt:
Formula E Gen4 test and development driver James Rossiter believes the new machine will be faster than F1 cars in wet conditions thanks to the new 'typhoon tyre.'

In recent years, F1 cars have seldom used the full wet tyres during green flag running in such conditions.

Rather, the blue-walled Pirelli tyres have been used under safety car periods or when grands prix have started behind the safety car, before drivers immediately switch across to the green-walled intermediate rubber.

This scenario played out after the long red flag delay at the 2022 Japanese GP, where drivers immediately bailed from the full wet tyre to the intermediates once green flag running resumed.

Bridgestone is returning as a tyre supplier to an FIA world championship in 2026, as it joins forces with Formula E for its all-new Gen4 era, with the cars capable of producing around 815bhp - or 600kw of energy.

Speaking when asked by RacingNews365 at a Q&A session at the unveiling of its Formula E tyres in Rome, Rossiter who has sampled the Gen4 machine in a variety of conditions indicated that the new 'typhoon tyre' would see FE machines faster than F1 in wet weather.

"With the typhoon tyre, I am willing to say this on record, that if it rains heavily, and you have a Formula 1 car on a full wet tyre, and I, a 43-year-old man, went out in a Gen4 car with a set of Bridgestones on it, I'm very confident that I'm comfortably faster than a Formula 1 car in the wet," Rossiter said.

"I think that the technology that Gen4 has, but also what Bridgestone have made in terms of the typhoon tyre, is truly remarkable with the amount of work that they put into it.

"You will see cars driving on circuits where the FIA would normally always put a red flag or end the session or do something, and the [Formula E] drivers will be perfectly happy.

"The drivers will be complaining this time that they want to drive, whereas in the past they were having the opposite. So we've got a very exciting transition point, I would say, in terms of the championship.

"In terms of steps forward, we've really created something spectacular with Gen4, and in collaboration with Bridgestone, we're able to put all that performance on the road in every condition."

title: Sebastian Vettel hitches a ride from F1 rival after bizarre post-race crash
excerpt:
Ahead of Formula 1's return to Sepang this weekend, RacingNews365 is revisiting some of the most dramatic moments the Malaysian Grand Prix has produced.

Few were as bizarre as Sebastian Vettel's slow-down lap collision with Lance Stroll in 2017.

Vettel had fought back from the rear of the grid to finish fourth for Ferrari after a difficult qualifying, with Max Verstappen taking victory for Red Bull ahead of Lewis Hamilton and Daniel Ricciardo.

But the drama did not end at the chequered flag.

On the cool-down lap, Vettel tried to pass Stroll's Williams around the outside at Turn 5.

The rookie drifted wide, and the pair made heavy contact that wrecked the left-rear suspension of Vettel's Ferrari, leaving the four-time champion stranded out on track.

[Article continues below]

A furious reaction over the radio

Vettel did not hide his frustration in the immediate aftermath, telling his team over the radio: "Stroll just drove into me. I mean, seriously."

He later gave his version of events: "I went on the outside to pick up a bit of rubber. I think Lance was trying to do the same thing, but wasn't looking and decided to turn in, so I was already there."

Stroll saw it rather differently, stating: "I was on the in-lap, on my normal line, picking up rubber, doing all my switch changes, shutting down the car and Sebastian came flying by me, pushing round the outside like the race was still on."

The FIA stewards investigated the clash and decided neither driver was predominantly at fault, with no penalties issued to either man.

With his Ferrari beyond repair, Vettel had to find another way back to the pits.

In an incident that is rarely seen in F1 due to the obvious dangers, Vettel clambered aboard the sidepod of Pascal Wehrlein's Sauber, hitching a ride for the remainder of the lap.

Wehrlein explained his decision to stop in a German television interview after the race: "For a friend like Sebastian, of course, I brake. I didn't even know what happened before."

It was far from the first time an F1 driver has needed a lift home.

Nigel Mansell famously carried Ayrton Senna back to the pits on his Williams FW14 at the 1991 British Grand Prix after Senna ran dry.

At the 2013 Singapore Grand Prix, Fernando Alonso picked up a stranded Mark Webber, earning both men a reprimand from the stewards.

title: Lando Norris delivers 'chaotic' prediction as F1 returns to Malaysia
excerpt:
F1 is heading back to Malaysia this weekend for the first time in nine years.

Lando Norris has predicted that the grand prix around the Sepang International Circuit this weekend will be a "chaotic" showcase.

The Asian track is making its first appearance on the F1 schedule in nine years, albeit under the Bahrain Grand Prix title, rather than Malaysia.

The sport has undergone significant changes since its last visit to the region and is currently in the first year of a new regulation cycle.

With the batteries having a major say in the wheel-to-wheel battles this year, overtakes have been aplenty at the energy-starved tracks.

Norris thinks this will be the case once again in Sepang this weekend, suggesting it could have similarities to the events at Monza.

"Honestly, I think next weekend [in Malaysia] will be pretty chaotic in terms of racing because of the straights and corner setup that you have there.

"So next weekend you'll see, in some ways, a similar vibe to Monza in some ways."

Driver

Lando Norris

British

1

Norris recalls previous Sepang experience

More than half of the grid did not race in Malaysia the last time it was on the circuit in 2017.

Despite arriving to the sport two years after it dropped from the calendar, Norris detailed that it is not completely new to him.

"I'm excited for it," he said. "I've seen many races of it when I was younger.

"I remember doing sim support for Fernando and Stoffel when they raced there many years ago. I remember going into the factory at midnight, or whatever stupid time it was, and driving until 7 AM just to support the guys.

"So it's not like I'd say completely new to me, but it'll be a first time going to the circuit itself, which is exciting.

"The only thing that's not exciting is because you have no battery. The two high-speed corners that should be high-speed, you run out of battery.

"That takes away a little bit of the character that I think you should have at such an incredible track.

"Otherwise, it's a new place, and I'm looking forward to another new challenge."

title: Why Esteban Ocon should and shouldn't make F1 return after Haas chop
excerpt:
RacingNews365 takes a look at whether Esteban Ocon can fight his way back onto the F1 grid in the future, or whether time will be called on his grand prix career.

30 September 2:45PM

That Esteban Ocon will leave Haas at the end of the 2026 season is no great surprise, with the Frenchman and the team coordinating their statements on Wednesday morning.

After two seasons, the one-time grand prix winner will leave the squad, but enters what he called "free agency" in Azerbaijan at an uncertain time.

Ocon may re-appear on the grid in the future, but one thing is certain. He will not be racing in F1 in 2027, in a full-time capacity at least.

With the news that Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll are staying on at Aston Martin for 2027, it reduced the number of available seats for 2027 to six across three teams.

One of these teams was Haas itself, which has just let Ocon go so he is not going to turn up there, which leaves Mercedes and Racing Bulls as the only places for a race seat.

Ocon, once the next cab off the Mercedes rank, will not be displacing George Russell and certainly won't be taking over the tenancy rights of the cockpit of the likely reigning world champion going into 2027 in Kimi Antonelli.

He has a next-to-zero chance of arriving at Racing Bulls, which already has its own 'three into two doesn't go' conundrum with incumbents Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad trying to fend off F2 protege and title contender Nikola Tsolov.

The best Ocon can hope for is to secure a third and reserve driver role with a team in 2027 with eyes on returning to the grid for 2028. As a capable, dependable hand, should any team require an injury or ban substitute in 2027, a driver with over 200 grands prix and experience of the 2026 power units would be an ideal choice.

This then puts Ocon firmly in the shop window for a full-time 2028 return - but has he done enough to warrant that or is his F1 career coming to a close?

© XPBimages

Why Ocon's time is over

Ocon is not the worst driver in F1, but neither is he an absolute world-beater who makes the case for dropping him one the bosses only briefly entertain.

He is a perfectly capable midfield F1 driver, capable of bagging decent results on his day, but his day has been relatively few and far between.

As an established driver with a grand prix win, four podiums, and as of the 2026 Azerbaijan GP, 195 starts. He is no rookie and has driven for three teams across a variety of regulations. He is not a mug.

With that level of experience, he should be the undisputed Haas team leader, comfortably leading his team in the midfield and performing well in the head-to-heads against his team-mate, a bit like old rival Pierre Gasly is at Alpine. There, there is no doubt about who the senior driver is.

But at Haas, Oliver Bearman has shown himself to certainly have Ocon's number. In qualifying in 2026, Bearman leads 10-5, with an average advantage of 0.206s, although Ocon does have the slightly better position of 14.7 to Bearman's 14.8.

In races where both have finished, Bearman is ahead 8-5 and has scored 20 points to Ocon's seven thus far.

At the absolute heart of the decision to drop Ocon is that he simply has not shown enough consistent performance to ensure Ayao Komatsu and Gene Haas seriously considered other options. He is a driver who does not bring a huge amount of sponsorship money, but this can be looked past if you are performing strongly and driving the team technically forward.

If you are not, as Ocon has found out, someone else will take your seat - with that someone believed to be either Ferrari F2 protege Rafael Camara or Haas's own third driver Jack Doohan - who both seriously impressed during recent TPC outings.

After nine-and-a-half seasons bouncing around the midfield and popping up with the odd podium or eye-catching drive, Ocon has essentially shown what he is. He is a known quantity, there are no surprises to him. After leaving Alpine in 2024 after falling out with management, Haas gave him another chance, with Komatsu personally determined to sign him.

Ocon has, on occasion, rubbed up team-mates and management the wrong way - most famously with Alonso at the 2022 Sao Paulo GP and with Gasly and Alpine bosses in Monaco 2024. Whilst he would argue he is just being himself, sometimes, the wider F1 game needs to be recognised and played.

But if Haas then decides that you are not the answer to their questions, where do you go? As Ocon has found out, you fall off the grid.

Why Ocon deserves another chance in F1

It is important to state that Ocon has not been able to showcase his true performance at Haas this term, and even in the second-half of 2025.

In 2025, he was struggling with the feel and bite of the brakes, before Haas, still one of the smallest operations on the grid, took a step backwards in the first year of the all-new regulations this season.

As well as being out-developed, the team, and both Ocon and Bearman have struggled with parts inconsistency and have swapped parts between them in a bid to try to unlock any drop of performance.

It appears, however, that an upgrade at Monza, coinciding with the use of the new Ferrari ADUO power unit, has boosted the car back into points contention.

Ocon finished eighth last time out in Azerbaijan, being pipped to equaling his best result since fifth in the 2025 Chinese GP by Lindblad by just 0.030s on the line, as Bearman was ninth.

It proves that when the car is capable of scoring strong points, Ocon can deliver it. He also showed great awareness at Turn 1 on the safety car restart as Colapinto turned the braking zone into a bowling alley, scoring a strike against team-mate Gasly and McLaren's Lando Norris.

Ocon is not a driver who throws the car at the scenery often and is more than prepared to defend himself on-track, even going toe-to-toe with the wily operator that is Alonso when they were Alpine team-mates.

Over the final eight races of the 2026 season, he also has a powerful tool that others seeking a route onto the F1 grid do not have: he has a race seat.

Between now and the final lap in Abu Dhabi, in this new points-scoring Haas, Ocon has the potential to sell himself and put himself, blinking lights and all, in the shop window for a reserve role in 2027 and a full-time seat elsewhere for 2028.

If he can best Bearman between now and the end of the campaign, he'll have a body of work to show potential suitors, and as the old adage goes, you are only as good as your last race. When it comes to 2028 silly season, that could be a very valuable pull factor for a team looking for a new driver - and a conversation Ocon should be in.

title: FIA declares heat hazard as F1 prepares for gruelling physical test
excerpt:
The FIA has declared a heat hazard for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, triggering additional measures for F1 drivers ahead of Sunday's race at Sepang International Circuit.

The governing body confirmed the decision under Article B1.5.10 of the 2026 F1 Sporting Regulations after the Official Weather Service forecast a Heat Index above 31.0°C during the race.

The declaration means teams must fit the components of the Driver Cooling System to their cars, with the system functional and available for use during the race.

Drivers can choose not to wear the cooling equipment itself, although additional ballast is then required. A five-kilogram Heat Hazard Mass Increase also applies for the race.

The measures are particularly significant at Sepang, which presents one of F1's most demanding combinations of heat, humidity and sustained high-speed running.

The 5.543-kilometre circuit features long straights, heavy braking zones and fast, flowing corners, requiring drivers to work hard physically while coping with the effects of Malaysia's tropical climate.

Sepang is often described as a complete test, with its heat and humidity adding significantly to the challenge.

The circuit's weather can also change rapidly, with thunderstorms and heavy rain capable of arriving at short notice.

F1's heat-hazard regulations were introduced following the extreme conditions at the 2023 Qatar Grand Prix, where several drivers suffered from heat exhaustion. The cooling system uses a chilled fluid circulated through equipment incorporated into the driver's protective clothing.

title: Ominous Mercedes upgrade causing unease amongst rival F1 teams
excerpt:
Mercedes underlined once again at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix that its rivals have still not managed to properly close the gap to the W17, despite minimal development on the car throughout the season so far.

That is even more significant when considering the power unit has run in its original specification all year, without the benefit of the ADUO 1 upgrade route granted by the FIA.

But the picture is about to change. For the Bahrain Grand Prix, held this weekend at the Sepang International Circuit in Malaysia, the W17 will carry a significant aerodynamic upgrade.

It is an evolution that is understood to be causing some unease among rival teams, not so much because of the scale of the package itself, but because of what it could mean for Mercedes' advantage over the field, particularly with a power unit upgrade still to come.

More load, more consistency

Sources close to the project indicate that the W17 upgrade is designed to generate more load through the car's bodywork, making the car even more competitive through the corners than it already is on the straights.

Through the season, it has become clear just how much the power unit's performance has allowed the W17 to dominate the fastest sections of a lap without any real resistance, especially long straights, as Baku confirmed once again thanks to near-flawless energy management.

At the start of the year, the W17 was dominant almost everywhere. But as the European rounds arrived, it became apparent that twisty circuits with a high number of slow corners represented the car's least favourable conditions.

In those sectors, the benchmark car was the Ferrari SF-26.

That shift in the competitive picture through the season persuaded Mercedes' technical team at Brackley against making major changes to the car, in order not to upset its overall balance.

The decision to debut the planned upgrade at Sepang is instead intended to lay the groundwork for next year's car.

The changes, concentrated mainly around the floor, the sidepod shaping and the wing elements, are aimed primarily at increasing load generated from the floor, without compromising the W17's efficiency on the straights.

Anticipation among rival engineers to see the scale of the Sepang package is high.

The details will start to emerge from Friday.

title: 2026 F1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia - weather forecast
excerpt:
Formula 1 returns to Sepang this weekend for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, with hot and humid conditions expected to provide an additional challenge for the drivers and teams.

Friday is currently forecast to be the wettest day of the weekend, with temperatures reaching around 31-33°C.

Light showers are possible throughout the day, while the risk of heavier, thundery rain cannot be discounted. Winds should remain relatively light, with gusts of around 16mph possible.

That creates the potential for a tricky opening day, particularly if a shower moves across the Sepang International Circuit during either practice session.

The combination of heat, humidity and intermittent rain could also make track conditions change quickly.

Conditions are expected to become somewhat more settled on Saturday, with sunny intervals forecast and temperatures again reaching around 31°C.

There remains a chance of a shower, particularly earlier in the day, but the current outlook suggests qualifying should have a largely dry backdrop. Gusts could again reach approximately 16mph.

Sunday's race is also expected to be hot and humid, with temperatures around 31°C and sunny intervals.

However, the threat of rain will remain, with a chance of showers during the morning and into the afternoon. Gusts could reach around 17mph.

Sepang's tropical climate means the forecast can change rapidly, and the possibility of a thunderstorm will keep teams alert throughout the weekend.

With the Bahrain Grand Prix taking place in Malaysia for the first time, weather could prove an important variable at the Sepang International Circuit.
